chapters.title: The Beginning of Summer
content: Scout Finch lives in Maycomb, Alabama with her brother Jem and father Atticus.
The town is small and everyone knows everyone else's business.
Scout's mother died when she was very young.
Atticus is a lawyer who believes in justice and treating everyone equally.
Calpurnia, their housekeeper, helps raise Scout and Jem.
The story is told from Scout's perspective as she looks back.
Scout is six years old at the start of the story.
Jem is ten and often acts as the protector of his younger sister.
A mysterious neighbor named Boo Radley fascinates the children.
Boo Radley never leaves his house and is the subject of rumors.
The children have never seen Boo Radley in person.
Legend says Boo stabbed his father with scissors many years ago.
The children are both afraid of and intrigued by Boo Radley.
Dill, a visiting boy from Mississippi, arrives for the summer.

chapters.title: The Radley Games
content: Summer arrives and Dill becomes close friends with Scout and Jem.
The children become obsessed with the Radley house and its mystery.
Dill dares Jem to touch the Radley house's front door.
Jem accepts the dare despite his fear of Boo Radley.
Jem runs to the house and touches the front steps quickly.
The children believe they see movement inside the Radley house.
Scout notices a small shadow moving behind the curtain.
The children run away in fear and excitement.
They begin acting out stories about the Radley family.
Scout plays the role of various town gossips in their games.
Atticus scolds them for bothering the Radley family.
He tells them to respect other people's privacy and choices.
The children are warned to stay away from the Radley property.
Their curiosity about Boo Radley only grows stronger.

chapters.title: The First Day of School
content: Scout begins first grade with Miss Caroline Fisher as her teacher.
Miss Caroline is young and unfamiliar with Maycomb's ways.
She tries to use modern teaching methods that confuse the children.
Scout already knows how to read and write because of Atticus.
Miss Caroline tells Scout to stop reading at home.
She wants Scout to learn the correct way in school.
Scout is frustrated by her teacher's unreasonable demands.
A boy named Walter Cunningham has no lunch money.
Miss Caroline offers to lend him money to buy lunch.
Walter refuses the offer because his family cannot repay debts.
Scout explains the Cunningham family's situation to her teacher.
Scout is punished for knowing too much about other families.
The day ends with Scout feeling misunderstood and discouraged.
Atticus helps Scout understand the situation better.

chapters.title: The Lunch with Walter
content: Scout fights a boy named Cecil Jacobs on the playground.
Jem stops the fight and invites Walter Cunningham to lunch.
Walter comes to the Finch house for a simple meal.
Scout criticizes Walter's eating habits at the table.
Calpurnia scolds Scout for being rude to their guest.
Calpurnia explains that Walter's family lives differently.
Scout learns an important lesson about poverty and dignity.
Atticus discusses the Cunningham family with Scout.
He explains the cycle of poverty in Maycomb.
The Cunningham family works hard but cannot escape debt.
Scout begins to understand class differences in the town.
Jem is embarrassed by Scout's behavior at the table.
The children learn about empathy and understanding others.
Scout starts to see the world with more compassion.

chapters.title: The Radley's Knothole
content: Summer returns and Scout, Jem, and Dill play together daily.
They decide to leave a note for Boo Radley using a fishing pole.
The note invites Boo to come outside and talk with them.
Before they can deliver the note, Atticus catches them.
Atticus orders them to stop trying to contact Boo Radley.
The children continue to be fascinated by the Radley mystery.
Dill and Jem plan to sneak into the Radley property at night.
Scout is reluctant but agrees to go along with them.
They attempt to look into the Radley house through windows.
A gunshot suddenly rings out in the darkness.
The children run in terror, and Jem loses his pants.
Nathan Radley fires a shotgun at a shadow in his yard.
The children barely escape without being discovered.
Boo Radley remains as mysterious as ever.

chapters.title: The Gifts in the Tree
content: Jem returns to the Radley property at night to retrieve his pants.
He finds the pants mended and folded neatly by the fence.
Jem is shocked that someone fixed the pants for him.
The children discover a knothole in the Radley's oak tree.
They find sticks of chewing gum wrapped in foil inside.
Later, they discover two carved soap figures inside the knothole.
The carvings look like Scout and Jem themselves.
The children realize Boo Radley is leaving these gifts for them.
They leave a thank you letter in the knothole.
More gifts appear: an old pocket watch and a spelling medal.
The children decide that Boo Radley is not a monster.
He is trying to befriend them through the knothole.
Nathan Radley fills the knothole with cement.
He claims the tree is sick and needs to be protected.

chapters.title: The Fire
content: Winter arrives in Maycomb with unusual cold weather.
Mrs. Radley dies during the winter season.
Nathan Radley and Boo's father pass away that winter.
The children wonder what will happen to Boo now.
Miss Maudie's house catches fire one cold night.
The whole town gathers to help fight the fire.
Scout and Jem watch the fire from a safe distance.
The fire destroys Miss Maudie's house completely.
Scout wears a blanket that someone placed around her shoulders.
She does not know who gave her the blanket during the fire.
Jem realizes that Boo Radley gave Scout the blanket.
Boo came outside to protect Scout from the cold.
The children are amazed by Boo's kindness and courage.
Boo Radley proves that he is a protector, not a monster.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
content: Atticus agrees to defend Tom Robinson, a black man accused of rape.
The town is angry that Atticus is taking the case seriously.
Scout and Jem face taunts from other children at school.
Atticus tells his children to hold their heads high.
He explains that everyone must live with their conscience.
The trial is about justice versus prejudice.
Scout does not fully understand the trial's significance.
Jem is old enough to feel the tension in the town.
Atticus's decision puts the entire family in danger.
The town divides between those who support and oppose Atticus.
Scout overhears hurtful comments about Atticus.
She asks Atticus about the insults people are saying.
Atticus teaches Scout about courage and integrity.
The children watch as their father stands firm in his beliefs.

chapters.title: The Courthouse
content: The day of the trial finally arrives in Maycomb.
Scout, Jem, and Dill sneak into the courthouse to watch.
The courthouse is packed with spectators from all over.
Tom Robinson sits in the courtroom looking terrified.
Mayella Ewell accuses Tom Robinson of assaulting her.
Atticus questions each witness carefully and thoroughly.
He shows that the evidence does not match Mayella's story.
Tom Robinson's left arm is crippled from a childhood accident.
He could not have physically committed the crime as described.
Atticus reveals that Mayella was attacked by her own father.
Bob Ewell, Mayella's father, is known as the town drunk.
Atticus proves that Bob Ewell is lying about the incident.
The jury does not believe the evidence against Tom Robinson.
Prejudice overcomes the truth in the hearts of the jury.

chapters.title: The Verdict
content: The jury returns with a guilty verdict for Tom Robinson.
The courtroom erupts with mixed reactions of anger and joy.
Atticus is devastated by the outcome of the trial.
The verdict was expected because of deep racial prejudice.
Tom Robinson is sent to prison despite being innocent.
The black community shows immense respect for Atticus.
Tom Robinson tries to escape from prison and is shot and killed.
His death is considered a tragedy by everyone who knew him.
Scout and Jem are deeply affected by the injustice.
Atticus teaches them to live with moral courage.
Bob Ewell spits on Atticus in public after the trial.
Ewell makes threats against Atticus and his family.
The family fears for their safety in the following days.
Scout begins to understand the cruelty of the world.

chapters.title: The Halloween Night
content: Halloween arrives in Maycomb with a school pageant.
Scout performs in the pageant dressed as a ham.
The pageant runs late and the children walk home in the dark.
They hear strange sounds on the way back to their house.
Scout and Jem are attacked in the darkness.
Jem is seriously injured during the violent assault.
Scout cannot see who is attacking them in the darkness.
A mysterious man appears and pulls the attacker away.
Scout discovers that Bob Ewell is their attacker.
The mysterious man fights Ewell to protect the children.
The sheriff arrives and finds Ewell dead with a knife.
Scout realizes that Boo Radley saved them from Ewell.
Boo Radley emerges from the shadows and speaks to Scout.
Scout is no longer afraid of Boo Radley.

chapters.title: The Truth Revealed
content: Boo Radley carries the injured Jem to the Finch house.
Atticus is shocked and grateful to Boo for saving his children.
The sheriff explains that Ewell was killed in the struggle.
The community is shaken by the attempted murder of children.
Scout stands on the Radley porch and sees the world anew.
She finally understands the story from Boo Radley's perspective.
Boo has been watching over Scout and Jem their entire lives.
Scout takes Boo's hand and walks him home.
She sees the places where Boo has been hiding all these years.
Scout realizes that Boo Radley is a kind and gentle person.
The town's rumors were completely wrong about Boo.
Scout learns the importance of not judging others.
Jem recovers from his injuries slowly.
Scout tells Atticus about everything that happened.

chapters.title: The Reflections
content: Scout walks Boo Radley home and says goodbye to him forever.
She stands on his porch and sees the neighborhood through his eyes.
Boo has been watching Scout and Jem grow up from his window.
He has been silently protecting them all along.
Scout finally understands her father's teachings about empathy.
The story concludes with Scout's reflections on the events.
She learns that courage exists in many forms.
Boo Radley was a mockingbird who never harmed anyone.
Tom Robinson was another mockingbird destroyed by prejudice.
Scout realizes that people are not always what they seem.
The world is filled with both cruelty and kindness.
Scout grows up significantly through these experiences.
She learns to see the world with compassion and understanding.
The book ends with Scout remembering her father's words.
